papers.title: Lunar tidal response-induced clock frequency variations on the Moon
papers.abstract: As clock performance improves, the instability and uncertainty of the clock's fractional frequency shift (FFS) become comparable to the FFS caused by the lunar tidal response (LTR), so the influence of the LTR on lunar time needs to be investigated. In this paper, we used the Keplerian expansions method to study the FFS to the level of $10^{-18}$ caused by the LTR between two clocks placed in different positions on the Moon. We consider the case of the Moon orbiting in an elliptical orbit, which is closer to the actual situation compared to the case of the Moon moving in a circular orbit. An interesting phenomenon is found that the longitude difference between two clocks can cause a change in the amplitude and phase of the FFS due to the LTR, but the latitude difference only changes the amplitude of the FFS. We further estimated the clock difference between two clocks near the Moon caused by the LTR. When one clock is on the lunar surface, and the other is on the Earth's surface, the LTR will cause a clock difference of $% -5.68\times 10^{-7}$ $\mu $s/day between the two clocks. These are significant for the construction of a lunar time and clock synchronization near the Moon.

papers.title: Development of an FPGA-Based Readout System and Functional Characterization of a Custom NSX1 ASIC for X-ray instrumentation
papers.abstract: We developed an FPGA-based readout system for a front-end ASIC (NSX1) with 64 channels to read out a large- area silicon drift detector used in X-ray detection instruments such as the Wide Field Monitor module for the STROBE-X mission concept. The FPGA acts as a central controller for the NSX1 configuration, implementing trigger handling and event sequencing, precise event timestamping, control of an external ADC for digitization, and data transfer to the host PC. The system enables comprehensive ASIC characterization; here, we demonstrate preliminary ASIC functionality and characterization tests using a calibrated pulser for two programmable linear gain responses of 375 mV/fC and 750 mV/fC. These preliminary results validate the low-noise performance of the NSX1 ASIC and demonstrate successful integration of the DAQ system.

papers.title: Unconventional Materials for Light Dark Matter Detection
papers.abstract: We propose the use of several unconventional materials as detectors for dark matter with mass beneath the MeV scale. These include the transition-metal dichalcogenide TiSe$_2$ hosting a low-energy plasmon in the charge-density-wave phase, Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ containing a low-energy acoustic demon mode, and hole-doped diamond with tunable optical and acoustic plasmon frequencies. We perform first-principles density functional theory computations of their loss functions at non-vanishing momenta and establish their reach into light dark matter parameter space. We show that due to intense low-energy plasmon modes -- of different microscopic origin in each -- the reach of detectors based on these materials could surpass existing proposals by several orders of magnitude for both dark matter scattering and absorption on electrons. The anisotropic response of these materials, which enables directional detection, renders them exceptionally strong detector candidates, motivating the design and fabrication of future devices.

papers.title: Radiation hardness characterization of SiPM sensors for Low Earth Orbit space missions
papers.abstract: This work presents a comprehensive radiation hardness characterization of SiPM devices for space-based applications: FBK NUV-HD-MT and NUV-HD-LowCT (1$\times$1, 3$\times$3, and 6$\times$6~mm$^2$) and Hamamatsu S14160 MPPCs with equivalent active areas. Total Ionizing Dose (TID) tests were performed at the ESA/ESTEC Co-60 facility with a level of dose up to 20~krad in silicon, while displacement damage effects were evaluated using 100~MeV protons with a fluence up to $1.12\times10^{11}$~p/cm$^2$ at the Paul Scherrer Institute. Radiation damage in SiPMs manifests through two main mechanisms: ionizing energy loss and non-ionizing energy loss (NIEL), which increases dark current and dark count rate. In this work, breakdown voltage, dark current, and quenching resistance were systematically measured as functions of accumulated dose and fluence. Gain and dark count rates were indirectly measured from the characterized electrical parameters. Both technologies exhibit remarkable stability of most of the functional parameters across all dose levels, while dark current shows predictable increases significantly more pronounced under proton irradiation due to displacement damage. Based on these results, both FBK and Hamamatsu devices are confirmed suitable for Low Earth Orbit (LEO) mission environment.

papers.title: Femtosecond Three-Dimensional Imaging of Single-Protein with Hard X-ray Laser
papers.abstract: The extreme intensity of X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) pulses has enabled imaging of radiation-sensitive samples, such as macromolecular microcrystals, beyond radiation damage limits. These sources have the potential to enable biomolecular single-particle imaging, similar to cryo-electron microscopy but without the need for cryo-fixation and with temporal resolution from femtoseconds to milliseconds. While this possibility was recognized before XFELs were built, the biological single-particle imaging work flow has previously only been demonstrated on large virus particles. Building on improvements in X-ray beam focusing, particle delivery, diffraction detection, and advanced analysis, here we demonstrate imaging of a single molecular complex, the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses. Two-dimensional classes of diffraction patterns could be reconstructed to 15 Angstrom resolution, and 3D images to ~20 to 30 Angstrom, even though the 3D merged intensity in reciprocal space extended beyond 20 Angstrom. The resolution discrepancy is likely due to heterogeneity caused by gas-phase compaction of the complexes. With increased throughput, this approach could be used to reveal in-situ structural details during mass spectrometry studies of biomolecules, while improvements in sample delivery may provide ultrafast snapshot imaging of biological single-particles in their native-state beyond the limitations of radiation damage.

papers.title: Preparing State-Selected Molecular Beams with high Efficiency using Quantum Cascade Lasers
papers.abstract: We demonstrate the ro-vibrational state-selective preparation of CO molecules ($v$ = 0, J = 0 $\rightarrow$ $v$ = 1, J = 1) in an internally cold molecular beam using a continuous-wave, narrow-linewidth distributed feedback type quantum cascade laser, with an output wavelength of 4.65 $\mu$m. Using a modulation-free wavelength stabilization scheme, we show that population transfer to near saturation levels can be obtained with sufficient long term stability, as needed for state-resolved scattering experiments. We show preliminary results of CO molecules prepared in the $v$ = 1 state, scattering from a clean Cu(100) surface. This study showcases the promise of QCL based excitation for state-selected molecular beam based scattering experiments, especially involving transitions in the mid-infrared domain ($\lambda$ > 4.5 $\mu$m) which are otherwise difficult to access using conventional sources.

papers.title: Beam performance and data-constrained optical modeling of a UV-transmitting acrylic Cherenkov counter for hadron identification
papers.abstract: A threshold Cherenkov counter based on ultraviolet-transmitting (UVT) acrylic has been developed for hadron identification in the S-2S spectrometer at J-PARC. Three 730 mm $\times$ 100 mm $\times$ 50 mm radiators were beam tested: polished UVT acrylic without WLS, UVT acrylic roughened on the four long surfaces without WLS, and polished UVT acrylic containing 10 ppm by mass bis-MSB as a wavelength shifter (WLS). The polished/WLS prototype gave the largest two-ended photoelectron yield among the tested configurations. At a 1-photoelectron software-SUM threshold, its measured detection efficiency remained above 99% throughout the scanned longitudinal range, with no significant degradation up to an average extracted-particle rate of approximately $2.5\times10^{5}~{\rm s^{-1}}$ during beam delivery. Beam observables constrained a Geant4 optical model with one common detector response scale and no PMT-specific response tuning. The model reproduces the observed response hierarchy and main longitudinal trends. In the central |y| < 200 mm region, simulated and measured MPV estimators for the calibration configurations typically agree within about 15%, while larger deviations occur toward the radiator ends, especially for rough/no-WLS. With the calibrated parameters fixed, the model was used to compare unmeasured detector configurations and quantify the momentum dependence of $K^{+}$/p discrimination. In the central, normal incidence geometry, a 90% $K^{+}$-survival working point is predicted to keep proton survival below 3% up to about 1.8 GeV/c. The measurements and constrained extrapolations support the polished UVT/WLS configuration for S-2S and quantify its expected particle-identification reach beyond the simple threshold regime.

papers.title: The Intermediate Silicon Tracker Detector for sPHENIX
papers.abstract: A new barrel-type silicon detector has been constructed in the central rapidity region of the sPHENIX experiment as part of its charged-particle tracking system. The detector, referred to as the intermediate silicon tracker (INTT), provides single-event timing capability and contributes to charged-particle tracking in combination with the silicon-pixel vertex detector and the time-projection chamber. The INTT consists of two cylindrical barrels with full azimuthal coverage. The inner and outer barrels comprise 24 and 32 silicon strip ladders, respectively. Each ladder consists of four silicon strip sensors, covering the pseudorapidity range $|\eta| < 1.07$ for collision vertices within $\pm~10$ cm along the beam axis, at radial distances between 72 and 103 mm. The INTT has been fully integrated into the sPHENIX data acquisition system, with detector signals processed by eight FELIX servers. Continuous data taking is enabled by a streaming readout mode, in which detector data are accumulated without hardware triggers, while a conventional trigger-based mode is also supported. The detector achieves stable operation, small inactive area, and high efficiency, providing precise timing, tracking, and vertexing performance during the collection of beam-beam collision data.

papers.title: Automatic indexing of wide-band quasi-Laue neutron diffraction patterns of large unit cells
papers.abstract: With a continuous spectrum of incident neutron wavelengths, quasi-Laue diffraction records many Bragg reflections from a stationary crystal, each satisfying the diffraction condition at a particular wavelength. Because the wavelength of each reflection is not measured, the crystal orientation must be determined from the scattering directions alone. At the new IMAGINE-X instrument, instant-readout detectors and many short exposures per experiment require this indexing to run automatically, yet for a protein crystal at the full 2-10 Angstrom band a single peak can have approximately $10^4$ candidate reflections, and a random orientation indexes a large fraction of the observed peaks. We describe an algorithm that indexes such patterns for a known unit cell and wavelength band. Differential evolution searches uniformly sampled rotations, matching observed directions to band-limited shells of candidate directions, and each solution is tested against the indexing expected for a random orientation. In a benchmark search, a k-d tree and a persistent pool of 32 worker processes reduce the wall time 270-fold relative to a serial scan of all candidates. The algorithm is first validated on the time-of-flight diffractometer MANDI, where the measured wavelengths give a reference solution by standard indexing. With the wavelengths discarded, every indexed reflection from 93 rare-earth garnet patterns agrees up to harmonic order. The algorithm then reliably indexes the natural mineral mesolite, measured on the original image plate at IMAGINE before the upgrade, and the protein T4 lysozyme, measured on the new IMAGINE-X instrument over the full band.

papers.title: Particle transformers for identifying Lorentz-boosted Higgs bosons decaying to a pair of W bosons
papers.abstract: A novel deep neural network classifier, a ``Particle transformer'' (PaRT), is introduced for the identification of highly Lorentz-boosted resonances reconstructed as single, multipronged jets in measurements and searches performed by the CMS Collaboration at the CERN LHC. Based on a self-attention mechanism that allows the model to weigh the importance of different particles, PaRT is trained on a wide variety of topologies, notably demonstrating strong performance for the first time on jets originating from boosted Higgs boson decays to W bosons. The PaRT algorithm achieves a tagging efficiency of more than 50% for such jets at a background efficiency of 1%, while maintaining decorrelation from the jet mass. A calibration is performed in proton-proton collision data collected by CMS at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, with a data set corresponding to a total luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$. Data-to-simulation selection efficiency scale factors are measured to be in the 0.9$-$1.0 range, with relative uncertainties between 7 and 23%. The tagging capability of PaRT enhances the sensitivity of standard model measurements and searches for beyond-the-standard-model resonances decaying to hadronic diboson systems.

papers.title: Advancing optical imaging systems with digital fabrication
papers.abstract: Optical imaging technologies are central to discovery in the life and physical sciences, yet their impact depends on how readily they can be built, adapted, and sustained across laboratories. Digital fabrication, including desktop 3D printing, offers new ways to engineer imaging instruments by simplifying assembly, lowering replication barriers, and enabling modular integration and local refinement. Here we examine, using open microscopy as a transparent case, how digitally fabricated components support adaptable, research-grade optical systems while enabling faster innovation cycles and distributed improvement. We outline practical design guidelines and discuss emerging developments that may further advance accessible, high-performance imaging.

papers.title: Development of an Analog Front-End Using NINO ASIC for Mini-ICAL
papers.abstract: The mini-ICAL was supposed to be a pre-prototype detector of the Iron CALorimeter (ICAL) of the India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) project. Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) was the active element of these detectors. As this detector operates in avalanche mode, one needs a very fast pre-amplifier for signal processing. NINO ASIC developed for the ALICE time-of-flight detector was a potential chip to be used as the analog-front end. This paper presents an 8-in-1 pre-amplifier board developed using the NINO ASIC, a single-ended to differential signal conversion using the differential driver chip manufactured by Texas Instruments, production of the boards, lessons learned during production, testing of these boards, and interface with RPCs. Finally, its performance based on strip rates and efficiency of the detector will also be discussed.
